prose.article: In the New Testament εὐνοῦχος refers to a castrated man, rendered "eunuch" in 5 of 8 occurrences (63%). The word covers a range: a literally emasculated man, a court official like the chamberlain in Acts 8:27, and figuratively a man who chooses not to marry (Matthew 19:12). In the Septuagint it appears 34 times, almost always translating the Hebrew סָרִיס (28×), a term that, as Abbott-Smith notes, did not always mean a literal eunuch but could simply mean a court officer.
prose.caution: The word's exact force varies between literal castration, court office, and voluntary celibacy, and the underlying Hebrew סָרִיס was itself not always literal.

prose.article: εὐοδόω is built from "well" (εὖ) and "road" (ὁδός), so its root idea is having a good journey, and from there it broadens to prospering and succeeding in general. It appears 4 times across 3 books in the Byzantine New Testament — covering both the literal travel sense (Paul hoping his way to Rome will go well) and the figurative one (the wish in 3 John 2 that the reader may prosper). The Septuagint uses it heavily, 50 times, most often (36×) for the Hebrew צָלַח, "to prosper or succeed," and the papyri confirm the everyday travel sense, as in a letter praying that God will speed the writer's journey to his sister.
prose.caution: The New Testament evidence is thin (only 4 occurrences), and the literal-versus-figurative balance depends on context, though the lexicons and corpus data agree on the overall range.

The second use of ζεστός in this verse repeats the word in the same metaphorical contrast, confirming the figurative 'spiritually fervent' sense but also showing the word's entire NT usage is confined to this single pericope
